lessonTitle: Stress Concentration Factors: Holes, Fillets and Notches

blocks.text: In 1954 the de Havilland Comet airliners broke up in flight after a few thousand pressurisation cycles. Fatigue cracks started at the corners of cabin cut-outs, where the local stress was several times the average skin stress. A small geometric feature had multiplied the stress, and it is exactly this multiplication that a stress concentration factor measures.

blocks.markdown: Elementary formulas such as $\sigma=P/A$ assume a uniform stress field. Near a hole, notch, fillet or sudden change of section, the force flow is forced to bend around the discontinuity, **crowding** the stress locally. We characterise the peak by the **theoretical (elastic) stress concentration factor** $K_t$, defined with a **nominal stress** $\sigma_{nom}$ calculated by the elementary formula on the specified (usually net) section. We assume linear-elastic, isotropic material, static loading and that $K_t$ depends on geometry and loading type only, not on the material.

blocks.caption: Peak stress from the theoretical concentration factor

blocks.title: Nominal stress and which section it refers to
blocks.text: $\sigma_{nom}$ is not an agreed universal quantity. Charts state which section it refers to. For a plate with a hole, $\sigma_{nom}=P/[(w-d)t]$ (net section), with plate width $w$, hole diameter $d$ and thickness $t$. For a stepped shaft, $\sigma_{nom}$ is computed on the **smaller** diameter $d$ (tension $4P/\pi d^2$, bending $32M/\pi d^3$, torsion $16T/\pi d^3$).

blocks.title: Maximum stress at a hole in a finite-width plate
blocks.prompt: A flat steel plate, width $w=80$ mm and thickness $t=6$ mm, has a central circular hole of diameter $d=16$ mm and carries a tensile load $P=40$ kN. Use the typical chart-fit $K_t=3.00-3.14(d/w)+3.667(d/w)^2-1.527(d/w)^3$ based on net-section nominal stress. Find $\sigma_{max}$.

steps.text: Nominal stress on the net section.
For a typical yield strength of 275 MPa the local stress is close to yielding even though the nominal stress is only 104 MPa.

blocks.markdown: **Why a small circular hole in a wide plate gives $K_t=3$.** Kirsch's elasticity solution for a small circular hole of radius $a$ in an infinite plate with remote uniaxial tension $\sigma$ gives the hoop stress at the hole boundary $\sigma_\theta(a,\theta)=\sigma(1-2\cos2\theta)$, where $\theta$ is measured from the load direction. At $\theta=90^\circ$ (the sides of the hole transverse to the load) $\cos2\theta=-1$ and $\sigma_\theta=3\sigma$. At $\theta=0$ it is $-\sigma$ (compressive). Along the transverse axis, $\sigma_\theta(r)=\sigma[1+a^2/(2r^2)+3a^4/(2r^4)]$ falls from 3 at $r=a$ to about 1.22 at $r=2a$ and 1.07 at $r=3a$, so the concentration is **local** (Saint-Venant). Under equal biaxial tension the same method gives $K_t=2$.

blocks.markdown: **Reading a chart for a shoulder fillet.** For a stepped shaft with large diameter $D$, small diameter $d$ and fillet radius $r$, $K_t$ is read against $r/d$ for a curve labelled with $D/d$. A small fillet radius (sharp corner) gives a high $K_t$; a larger radius lowers it. The values below are typical chart readings for tension, with the nominal stress based on $d$; always use the chart that matches the loading (tension, bending or torsion) and the specified nominal stress.

blocks.title: Stress at a shaft shoulder
blocks.prompt: A stepped steel shaft has $d=30$ mm, $D=45$ mm and a shoulder fillet radius $r=3$ mm. It carries an axial tension $P=50$ kN. Find the maximum stress at the fillet, using the table above.

steps.text: Nominal stress on the small diameter.

items: Identify the geometry and loading (tension, bending, torsion) and find the matching chart or formula.
Note which section the nominal stress refers to and compute $\sigma_{nom}$ there.
Read or calculate $K_t$ from the geometric ratios.
Compute $\sigma_{max}=K_t\sigma_{nom}$ and compare with the strength (with the right failure criterion).

blocks.title: Wrong nominal stress, wrong answer
blocks.text: Using the gross-section stress with a net-section $K_t$ (or vice versa) can be wrong by 25% or more. Always check the definition printed on the chart.

blocks.title: $K_t$ depends on geometry only
blocks.text: The theoretical factor does not depend on the material or load magnitude in the elastic range. It is how sharply the geometry bends the force flow that matters.

points: The peak stress is $\sigma_{max}=K_t\sigma_{nom}$; $K_t$ depends on geometry and loading type and requires the correct nominal stress basis.
A small circular hole in a wide plate in uniaxial tension has $K_t=3$ (Kirsch: $\sigma_\theta=\sigma(1-2\cos2\theta)$); in equal biaxial tension $K_t=2$.
For a hole in a finite-width plate use net-section stress and a $K_t$ that depends on $d/w$; for shoulders read $K_t$ from $r/d$ and $D/d$ charts using the small-section nominal stress.
The concentration is local, decaying to the nominal stress within a few hole radii.

questions.stem: A very wide thin plate with a small circular hole is loaded in uniaxial tension $\sigma$ remote from the hole. Where is the maximum stress, and what is its value?

options.text: At the edge of the hole on the diameter perpendicular to the load, $3\sigma$
At the edge of the hole on the diameter parallel to the load, $3\sigma$
At the edge of the hole on the diameter perpendicular to the load, $2\sigma$

questions.correctOptionText: At the edge of the hole on the diameter perpendicular to the load, $3\sigma$

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Kirsch gives $\sigma_\theta=3\sigma$ at $\theta=90^\circ$ from the load axis.
distractorRationale.b: On the diameter parallel to the load the hoop stress is $-\sigma$ (compressive).
distractorRationale.c: $2\sigma$ is the factor for equal biaxial tension.
distractorRationale.d: The plate edges carry roughly the remote stress; the concentration is at the hole.

questions.explanation: From $\sigma_\theta=\sigma(1-2\cos2\theta)$ the maximum is at $\theta=90^\circ$, i.e. the points of the hole boundary across which the load flows, with value $3\sigma$. The stress decays to near $\sigma$ within about three hole radii.

questions.stem: A very wide plate with a small circular hole carries a uniform remote tensile stress of 85 MPa. Using the theoretical stress concentration factor, find the maximum stress at the hole in MPa.
questions.explanation: For a small circular hole in a wide plate $K_t=3$, so $\sigma_{max}=3\times85=255$ MPa. The remote stress is used because the plate is wide enough that the hole's net-section correction is negligible.

questions.stem: A flat plate of width 100 mm and thickness 5 mm has a central circular hole of diameter 20 mm and carries a tensile load of 30 kN. Take $K_t=3.00-3.14(d/w)+3.667(d/w)^2-1.527(d/w)^3$ based on the net section. Calculate the maximum stress in MPa.
questions.explanation: With $d/w=0.2$, $K_t=2.506$. The net-section nominal stress is $30000/(80\times5)=75$ MPa, so $\sigma_{max}=2.506\times75=188.0$ MPa.

questions.stem: A stepped shaft has $d=40$ mm, $D=60$ mm and a fillet radius $r=4$ mm, and carries an axial tension of 50 kN. Reading the lesson's table for $D/d=1.5$ at $r/d=0.10$, calculate the maximum stress at the fillet in MPa.
questions.explanation: Here $D/d=1.5$ and $r/d=0.10$, so $K_t=1.9$. The nominal stress on the small section is $4(50000)/(\pi 40^2)=39.79$ MPa, so $\sigma_{max}=1.9\times39.79=75.6$ MPa.

questions.stem: Using the lesson's chart readings for a shouldered shaft in tension with $D/d=1.5$, increasing the fillet radius from $r/d=0.05$ to $r/d=0.20$ changes $K_t$ from 2.4 to 1.6. By what percentage is the peak stress reduced (nominal stress unchanged)?

distractorRationale.b: Takes the difference 0.8 as a percentage, or divides by the wrong base.
distractorRationale.c: Halves the stress, which would need $K_t=1.2$.
distractorRationale.d: Takes the ratio 1.6/2.4 as the reduction; that is the remaining fraction, 67%.

questions.explanation: Peak stress is proportional to $K_t$ for fixed nominal stress, so the reduction is $(2.4-1.6)/2.4=33\%$. The remaining stress is 67% of the original, not the reduction.

questions.stem: Using the Kirsch result $\sigma_\theta=\sigma(1-2\cos2\theta)$ at the boundary of a small circular hole, explain why $K_t=3$ for uniaxial tension, state the stress at $\theta=0$, and explain what the decay of the stress away from the hole shows about the effect.
markingGuide: $\theta$ is measured from the load direction; the hoop stress at the boundary is $\sigma(1-2\cos2\theta)$.
Along the transverse axis the stress falls to about $1.22\sigma$ at $r=2a$ and $1.07\sigma$ at $r=3a$; the effect is local (Saint-Venant).
Physically the force flow lines must bend around the hole and crowd together at its sides.
questions.explanation: The factor 3 comes from the elasticity solution, not from a section-area argument, and is independent of hole size in a wide plate. A larger hole creates a larger region of high stress but the same peak factor.

questions.stem: A thin plate contains a narrow elliptical hole with semi-axis $a=12$ mm perpendicular to the load and $b=4$ mm along the load. The remote tensile stress is 40 MPa. Using the Inglis result $K_t=1+2a/b$, find the maximum stress at the ends of the ellipse in MPa.
questions.explanation: $K_t=1+2(12)/4=7$, so $\sigma_{max}=7\times40=280$ MPa. A circular hole ($a=b$) would give $K_t=3$, so an ellipse elongated across the load is much worse; this is why a crack is the extreme case.

questions.stem: A plate of width $w=100$ mm and thickness 5 mm has a hole of diameter 20 mm and carries 30 kN. A student calculates the nominal stress as $P/(wt)=60$ MPa for use with a net-section $K_t$ of 2.51. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The nominal stress should be 75 MPa on the net section, so $\sigma_{max}\approx188$ MPa, not 150 MPa
The student's calculation is correct because the gross area carries the load
The nominal stress should be $P/(\pi d^2/4)$ because the hole is circular
The nominal stress is irrelevant because $K_t$ already includes it

questions.correctOptionText: The nominal stress should be 75 MPa on the net section, so $\sigma_{max}\approx188$ MPa, not 150 MPa

distractorRationale.a: Correct: net area $=(100-20)(5)=400$ mm$^2$ gives 75 MPa.
distractorRationale.b: The chart-fit $K_t$ is defined on the net section; using the gross area underestimates the peak by 20%.
distractorRationale.c: The hole's area is not the load-bearing area; the remaining ligaments are.
distractorRationale.d: $K_t$ is a ratio, so a nominal stress on the stated basis is always required.

questions.explanation: A net-section $K_t$ must be multiplied by the net-section stress. Using the gross stress of 60 MPa gives 150 MPa, but the correct value is $2.51\times75=188$ MPa, an under-estimate of about 20% that would be unsafe.

questions.stem: A stepped steel shaft ($D=45$ mm, $d=30$ mm) carries an axial tension of 40 kN. Compare the peak fillet stress for a fillet radius of 1.5 mm and one of 6 mm, using the lesson's $D/d=1.5$ chart readings. State what the comparison shows about design.
markingGuide: Nominal stress on the small diameter $=40000/(\pi\times30^2/4)=56.6$ MPa.
A fourfold increase in radius reduces peak stress by 33%.
Conclusion: generous fillet radii (large $r/d$) are an effective, cheap way to lower the peak stress; sharp corners should be avoided.
questions.explanation: Peak stress is the product of an unchanged nominal stress and a geometry-dependent $K_t$, so only the fillet radius controls the difference. The two cases differ by the ratio 2.4/1.6=1.5.

questions.stem: True or false: for a small circular hole in a wide plate under equal biaxial tension $\sigma$ in both directions, the maximum stress at the hole boundary is $3\sigma$.
questions.explanation: Superposing the two uniaxial Kirsch solutions at right angles gives $\sigma_\theta=\sigma(1-2\cos2\theta)+\sigma(1+2\cos2\theta)=2\sigma$ at every point on the boundary. So $K_t=2$ for equal biaxial tension and 3 only for uniaxial tension.
